title: Sleep in peace (Psalm 4)
hook: a psalm for night prayer: in peace I will sleep and I will rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, two ways, and a tree planted by the water. Your line was roots near water. What fed your roots? Today, a psalm for the end of the day. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

It's one in the morning. The house is quiet, and your brain isn't. You're replaying a conversation from this afternoon, the thing they said, the thing you should have said back. You rehearse the perfect reply. Then you rehearse it again. You check the time. You turn the pillow over to the cool side. Most people know this bed very well. Long ago, somebody lay in it too, and wrote a song about it. The Church has been singing that song at bedtime for centuries.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `REPLAYING THE CONVERSATION.` → `A SONG FOR THAT BED.`

segments.voice: Psalm 4 is a night psalm. For centuries it was prayed at Compline, the Church's last prayer before sleep, and in today's Liturgy of the Hours it's still there on Saturday nights. It starts in trouble. "When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me." Enlarged: in Hebrew, God made room for me. Distress is a tight place, a narrow corner, and the prayer remembers a time God gave it space. Then comes the line for everyone lying awake angry. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be ye angry, and sin not: the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds." Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say don't be angry. It says be angry, and don't let the anger turn into harm. And those speeches you make in your head at one in the morning, the psalm tells you to take them to bed and let them go quiet there. Saint Paul quotes the first half of that line to the Ephesians, and adds his own: don't let the sun go down on your anger. The psalm ends with the line the whole night is waiting for: "In peace in the selfsame I will sleep, and I will rest." In the selfsame, meaning in the same moment, all at once. Not after everything is fixed. Not after you win the argument. The one praying has the same enemies and the same worries, and still decides to lie down and trust. Sleep, in this psalm, is an act of faith.
screen: `A NIGHT PSALM, PRAYED AT COMPLINE.` · `THOU HAST ENLARGED ME.` · `BE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.` · `SLEEP AS AN ACT OF TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line before sleep. Right now, settle and breathe, and find tonight's unfinished conversation, the one most likely to keep you up. Don't solve it. Just notice it, the way the psalm says: say it in your heart, and let it be quiet. Then practice the line you'll say tonight with the light off: in peace I will sleep, and I will rest. If you pray, you can say it to God. If you don't, let it be a way of putting the day down. The bell holds the time.
Sleep in peace. The last line of Psalm 4, a night prayer that lies down before everything is fixed. Today's word.
Your line: in peace I will sleep. Tonight, say it once in the dark, and let tomorrow's arguments wait until tomorrow. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours pray Psalm 4 at Night Prayer (Compline) on Saturday nights; for centuries it was part of Compline every night, the Church's last prayer before sleep.

original.note: Hebrew: in peace, the first word of the psalm's last verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle bedtime verse.
what it means: a night prayer from someone in real trouble, who lies down in peace before anything is fixed.
what a scholar hears: enlarged translates a Hebrew root for making wide, the opposite of distress, a narrow place; the psalm has been sung at Compline for centuries.

sources.ref: Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer after Evening Prayer I of Sunday

notes: Psalm 4 at Compline: daily in the older Roman Breviary; in the current Liturgy of the Hours after Evening Prayer I of Sunday (Saturday night). Confirm.
Douay verse numbering (4:2, 4:5, 4:9) and wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.
'Enlarged' as God making room: Hebrew rachav (to be wide), contrasted with tsar (narrow, distress). Confirm.
The psalm is not dated in the script (long ago).
